```{r setup, eval = FALSE}
library(plant)
source("harness/long_drought.R")   # rainfall records and mkenv()
p <- scm_base_parameters("TF24")
p <- add_strategies(p, trait_matrix(0.32, "lma"))
```

# The whole thing

A node schedule is a quadrature rule over birth date. It has two parts:

- **Breakpoints:** the births at which a recruit's fate changes slope abruptly. A
  first run finds them.
- **A node density** on the stretches between breakpoints, saying how closely nodes
  are spaced there.

A run estimates its own error. Replay it on its own steps with every other node
between breakpoints removed. A third of the change is the run's error in every
quantity. If any quantity is over its tolerance, raise the density and run again.
The last run is the answer.

```{r whole, eval = FALSE}
fit <- refine_schedule(p, mkenv("episodic"))
fit$answer     # ln J and its gradient, from the last run
fit$estimate   # each quantity's error, from that run's own replay
fit$where      # how the remaining error is spread over birth date
```

The sections below explain each part: what a node does, where fate changes slope,
where it curves, how a run measures its own error, and how the loop uses that.

# What a node is

On the birth-date coordinate a node is the cohort born at one instant. The
individuals born between two neighbouring nodes form an interval, and the interval
carries two things:

- **Its count.** The run integrates the establishment rate exactly over the interval,
  together with its first moment.
- **Its members' fate.** Their survival, size and output are taken to vary linearly
  in birth date between the two nodes.

Every stand total has the same form: J, the leaf area above a height, the water drawn
from a soil layer. Each is a sum over intervals of count × interpolated fate.

The schedule's error is the error of that quadrature. It has three properties that
everything else rests on:

- **Where fate is smooth, an interval's error is about count × width² × fate's
  curvature.** It falls four-fold when the spacing halves.
- **The error adds over birth date.** Regions refined one at a time add to the whole
  run's error within 0.04ε.
- **A local error travels.** An interval that over-counts leaf area or uptake shades or
  dries every other cohort, so its error shows up in all of them.

# Where fate changes slope: breakpoints

**Net production decides everything.** An individual's net production is

    P = a_bio · a_y · (A − R) − T

where A is the leaf's optimal assimilation, set by the light at its crown and the water
its roots reach. P drives each process:

- **P > 0:** the individual grows and fills its storage pool.
- **P < 0:** the pool drains, and the hazard a_dG1 · exp(−a_dG2 · r) rises as relative
  storage r falls.
- **Establishment:** a newborn establishes only if its P at seed height is positive.

A seedling's roots lie in the top 0.3 m of soil, so establishment follows the top
layer's water: a rain opens it within a day, and the stand's uptake dries the layer
until it shuts.

**At each opening, fate's slope jumps.**
- A cohort born just before an opening waits for rain, so a later birth waits less and
  does better.
- After the opening, each later cohort meets more shade, so it does worse.
- On dry, fate's slope was +0.5e-3 per day before every one of 22 openings and
  −2.2e-3 per day after.

**At a shutting, fate stays smooth.** Fate rises into the closed gap; the gate closes
over 1–2 days, and establishment is counted exactly either way.

**On constant rain there is one more slope jump.**
- Cohorts born in the first 23.5 days reach the canopy.
- Every later cohort stalls under them: its P falls below zero and comes back.
- Survival to the end of the run falls from 0.63 to 0.02 across 0.03 days of birth
  date.

Both kinds are found the same way. Fate changes slope only where a cohort's sequence of
P sign changes differs from its neighbour's. A first run records each node's count of
sign changes, and the establishment rate at every step:
- the counts change across every pair of neighbours that straddles an opening;
- on constant rain they go from 0 to 2 exactly at the stall.

A first run on about 100 even introductions places 98–100% of openings within a day.
On constant rain, five rounds of forward runs with about 100 nodes place the stall to
0.0003 day.

A breakpoint is a node that is never moved or removed. Put a node on every slope jump,
and every stretch between breakpoints is smooth: a spell, its shutting and the closed gap
that follows.

# Where fate curves: the node density

Between breakpoints fate is smooth, but it curves, and the density must follow the
curvature. Four shapes recur:

- **The first cohorts.** Births before the first shutting earn 70–97% of J. Their fate
  falls nearly exponentially in birth date, with a decay length of 0.4–1.2 years, because
  a later birth reproduces later in calendar time, against the patch's disturbance and the
  stand's drought mortality.
- **The understory.**
  - Within a spell, a later birth is a smaller copy that has had less time to die, so its
    leaf area is convex in birth date.
  - Straight lines between nodes over-count that leaf area by 0.5–1.1% (3–4% in the
    first years). The soil then runs drier for everyone, and the first cohorts carry most
    of that error as extra drought mortality.
- **Before each shutting.** The cohorts' sensitivity to the hydraulic traits changes
  fastest 9–12 days before the gate shuts, set by the seedling's starting reserves.
- **Late births.** They earn little J but still draw down the water. Late intervals
  wider than about 110–160 days leave the square law on the traits that act through the
  soil.

**A node's cost also depends on its birth date.** An early node lives for the rest of the
run, so the rows it adds fall with birth date.

The first density comes from the first run: graded by the offspring curve and by the J
still to be earned at each birth date. It names no fixed age, so it works for any
simulation length.

# How a run measures its own error

Remove every other node between breakpoints, and replay the run on its own steps. A
third of the change is the run's error, in every quantity at once:

    error ≈ (Q with every other node removed − Q) / 3

Why it can be trusted:

- **Every node between breakpoints is removed, so no error goes unseen.** There is no
  other kind of node.
- **Each removal merges two intervals of equal share.** Nodes are placed to share the
  density equally, so every removed node sits at the centre of what it merges, which is
  where the factor of 1/3 holds.
  - Off centre the factor is (l³ + (1 − l)³)/(3 l (1 − l)) for a node at fraction l.
  - Schedules built by adding nodes next to existing ones are full of off-centre pairs,
    which is why their removal estimates read a third to a half of the error.
- **The replay shares the run's steps,** so step-size choices add nothing to the
  difference.
- **The replay carries the field.** A removed node changes the light and water every
  cohort meets, and the replay includes that.
- **It is measured, not assumed.** On dry its estimate matched the errors measured by
  refinement with correlation 0.93–0.99 across the elasticities; on episodic with lma
  ×1.25, 0.996. Removing every region at once gives the sum of removing each alone
  (correlation 1.000).
- **Cost:** about 0.8 of a run.

**Where the error is.** Each run also reports a map from its own reverse sweep:
- J's error by stretch of birth date, to 0.03ε, for 7.5% more than the run;
- split between light and water, so it says which way a region's error travels.

**A check that costs nothing.** The replay gives J's error exactly; the map gives it to
first order. When the two disagree, the run is coarser than the square law needs, and
its estimate is not yet trusted.

# The loop

```
  first run (about 100 even introductions, forward only)
        │ openings, sign-change counts, offspring curve, J still to earn
        ▼
  breakpoints + first density
        │
        ▼
  run ──► replay with every other node removed ──► error of each quantity
        │                                           and the map of J's error
        ▼
  every quantity under its ε, and the replay agrees with the map?
        │ yes: this run is the answer
        │ no:  scale the density by √(worst error / ε) and run again
```

- **Every full run is a candidate answer;** no run is made only to be compared with.
- **It needs no tolerance from the user.** It stops at each quantity's ε.
- **It stops.** On the square law each scaling cuts the worst ratio by the square of the
  scale, and a cap on passes reports a failure instead of running on.
- **The density can follow the map** instead of rising everywhere. Whether that pays
  more than it risks is still being measured.

# What it adapts to

| what varies | why | what responds |
|---|---|---|
| when establishment opens | the rainfall record | breakpoints, from the first run |
| where fate curves | first cohorts, understory, before shutting, late births | the density |
| how large the error is | about 100× across trait × climate | the replay measures it on each run |
| which quantities bind | carbon traits in the first cohorts, hydraulic traits in the understory | every quantity has its own ε |
| how mechanisms interact | light and water carry a local error to every cohort | the replay includes the field; the map's split names the channel |
| what a node costs | early nodes live longest | the first density |
| simulation length | where J is earned | the first density, from J still to earn |
| coarse or unusual runs | near extinction, too coarse a start | the replay–map check refines once more |

# Traits

The traits move the breakpoints by moving where P = 0:
- Carbon gain, carbon cost and water access set the light and water at which P
  vanishes, and so when establishment opens.
- Height growth sets who ends up shaded.
- The storage pool sets how costly a spell below zero is.

On constant rain:
- lma ×0.8 and ×1.25 move the stall from day 23.6 to 27.1 and 18.9;
- hmat ×0.8 and ×1.25 move it to days 45–50 and 10–12.

A schedule refined at one θ serves nearby θ, but the error grows as θ moves. A moved
trait's error on the shared schedule costs one replay to measure, so each use can check
its own error.

# Still being tested

- that fate's slope jumps nowhere else;
- that the square law holds within a stretch at twice the spacing;
- that the density resolves the hydraulic change before each shutting at a cost near
  today's schedules; if not, a fixed node 12 days before each shutting is the next
  step;
- how much error sits in stretches too short to hold two nodes.
